label: Discriminants and Finite Type
notes: Open the lecture. A geometric viewpoint sees knots as points in a vast space, with singular knots forming a discriminant wall. The lecture uses this picture to motivate finite type invariants, setting up the definition by repeated differences across the discriminant that the next lectures develop fully.

label: The Space of Knots
notes: Think of all smooth embeddings of the circle as an infinite-dimensional space. Generic paths in it are isotopies, but special maps that fail to be embeddings, namely immersions with double points, form a codimension-one subset. Crossing this subset corresponds to changing a crossing in a diagram, the fundamental local move.

label: The Discriminant
notes: Define the discriminant as the set of singular knots, those with at least one transverse double point. It separates the space of knots into chambers, one for each knot type. Walls of the discriminant meet along higher singularities, and the combinatorics of these strata controls how invariants can jump from chamber to chamber.

label: Singular Knots and Differences
notes: Extend any knot invariant to singular knots by the difference rule: the value at a double point is the value of the positive resolution minus the negative resolution. This finite difference across the discriminant wall is the discrete derivative that measures how the invariant changes as a crossing is switched.

label: Toward Finite Type
notes: Call an invariant of finite type of order n if its extension vanishes on every singular knot with more than n double points. This says the invariant is polynomial of degree n in the crossing changes. Coefficients of the Conway and Jones polynomials, suitably expanded, supply the first examples.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. Viewing knots as chambers cut out by the discriminant of singular knots motivates measuring invariants by finite differences across crossing changes. An invariant is finite type of order n when enough differences kill it. This geometric setup launches Vassiliev's theory in the next lecture.
